tldr: This is a research trend, not one event: six unrelated arXiv papers in ten days each build an agent benchmark from real sessions, real tools or real fixes. It began with group-assistant memory (Nov 3), added MCP hallucinations and memory poisoning, then moved to long-horizon infra work, researcher workspaces and privacy-aware code review (Nov 13).
whats_new: The newest member (Nov 16) is a quantum recurrent-network benchmark for time-series prediction; it shares only the word "benchmarking", so PrivacyPR (Nov 13) remains the last agent-relevant entry.
why_it_matters: Each agent paper argues that standalone task scores overstate how agents behave on stateful, tool-heavy, long-horizon or compliance-sensitive work, which is the work platform teams actually deploy them on.

beats.headline: Group-assistant benchmark tests memory use, not just recall
beats.summary: Evaluates whether an assistant shared by many users turns remembered context into appropriate help when there is no fixed answer.

beats.headline: MCPHallu and MemoryDojo benchmark how agents break
beats.summary: One measures reasoning, execution and memory hallucinations in MCP tool use; the other tests whether malicious instructions persist through agent memory across sessions.

beats.headline: Infrathon and ARE-bench test agents on sustained real work
beats.summary: One asks whether agents keep improving real AI infrastructure over long horizons; the other scores research agents inside real researcher sessions and workspaces.

beats.headline: PrivacyPR targets privacy defects in agent code review
beats.summary: A dataset linking real privacy fixes to the defects they repaired, aimed at coding agents that review pull requests.

beats.headline: Quantum RNN time-series benchmark joins on a shared keyword
beats.summary: Quantum machine-learning research with no agent or platform angle; clustered here only by the word "benchmarking".

open_questions: Will any of these benchmarks publish a public leaderboard with frontier-model scores?
Which MCP hallucination type in MCPHallu do current agents fail most often: reasoning, execution or memory?
Does MemoryDojo show poisoned memory surviving into later sessions for the memory systems teams actually ship?
Do agents that score well on standalone suites rank lower on Infrathon or ARE-bench, as the authors suggest?
What share of PrivacyPR's real privacy defects do current coding-agent reviewers catch?
Will the datasets and harnesses be released openly enough to rerun as internal evals?
take_for_builders: If your agents persist memory or call MCP tools, add an eval that replays a poisoned instruction across sessions and logs tool-call hallucinations; keep gating rollouts on one eval built from your own logged sessions, not public scores alone.
